topic: Clean Repo Prompt Injection Defense Guide 2026: Protect AI Coding Agents Before Setup Scripts Run
keyword: clean repo prompt injection defense ai coding agents
overview: Comprehensive research on the 'Clean Repo' prompt injection attack vector targeting AI coding agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, OpenAI Codex) — where a repository with no obvious malicious payload tricks the agent into executing attacker-controlled code during routine setup steps. Covers the Mozilla 0DIN proof-of-concept (June 25, 2026), the Gemini CLI CVSS-10 supply chain attack, the arXiv systematic review of 78 studies, and a 10-layer defense-in-depth framework for protecting AI coding agents before setup scripts run.

problem_statement.summary: The 'Clean Repo' attack exploits a fundamental trust gap: AI coding agents read project files (README, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, setup.py, requirements.txt, package.json) as trusted instructions, but these files originate from untrusted external sources. In the Mozilla 0DIN PoC (June 25, 2026), a normal-looking Python repository caused Claude Code to install requirements, encounter a routine initialization error, and run the suggested fix — which queried a DNS TXT record, decoded the value, and executed it as a shell command, opening a reverse shell. Because the payload was fetched at runtime, static scanners, code reviewers, and dependency audits had nothing to flag. A January 2026 systematic review of 78 studies found adaptive prompt-injection attacks bypass many published defenses when attackers tune payloads to evade them. A study of agentic coding editors analyzed 314 prompt-injection payloads across 70 MITRE ATT&CK techniques and found success rates as high as 84% for malicious command execution against GitHub Copilot and Cursor.
attack_vectors: Indirect prompt injection via README.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or .cursorrules files
Setup script poisoning: agent follows documented install steps that trigger malicious commands
DNS TXT record payload delivery: final command fetched at runtime, invisible to static analysis
Package manager dependency confusion: malicious packages in requirements.txt/package.json
MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool poisoning: malicious tool definitions that execute commands
Error message exploitation: agent 'helpfully' runs suggested fix from fabricated error output
affected_tools: Claude Code (Anthropic) — AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md file-based skill definitions
GitHub Copilot — TypeScript-based extensions with marketplace distribution
Cursor — JSON/MCP-based skill definitions, no sandboxing
OpenAI Codex — MCP-based tool definitions, no sandboxing
Gemini CLI — supply chain attack via extension ecosystem (CVSS-10)

competitors.title: AI Agent Prompt Injection Defense: 2026 Production Security Playbook — Lushbinary
key_points: OWASP ranks prompt injection as #1 LLM vulnerability, affecting 73% of production deployments
10-layer defense-in-depth framework for AI agent prompt injection
Layer 1-2: Input Validation (sanitize all external content) + Output Filtering (validate tool calls against allowlist)
Layer 3-4: Privilege Separation (least-privilege service accounts) + Sandboxing (Docker/gVisor/Firecracker with --network=none, --read-only)
Layer 5-6: Content Boundary Markers (delimiters between trusted instructions and untrusted data) + Instruction Hierarchy (system > app logic > user > external data)
Layer 7-8: Canary Tokens (honeytokens that trigger alerts if accessed) + Rate Limiting (per-session and per-minute caps)
Layer 9-10: Anomaly Detection (ML-based behavioral monitoring) + Human-in-the-Loop (approval gates for high-risk actions)
OpenAI April 2026 Defense Guide: instruction hierarchy, structured output validation, content boundary markers

key_strategies.name: Pre-Scan Repository Before Agent Execution
key_strategies.description: Before any AI coding agent reads or executes commands from a repository, scan it for prompt injection indicators: embedded instructions in README/AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules, suspicious setup scripts, DNS/network call patterns in install steps, and known malicious patterns. Treat every unfamiliar repository, setup script, package file, and README as untrusted input.
key_strategies.implementation: Implement a pre-flight scanner that checks: (1) AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md for instruction override patterns, (2) setup.py/package.json for unexpected network calls, (3) README for embedded shell commands, (4) dependency URLs for typosquatting. Block execution if any trigger fires.

key_strategies.name: Sandboxed Execution with Network Isolation
key_strategies.description: Execute all agent actions in isolated environments with no network access, read-only filesystem, and strict resource limits. Even if an injection succeeds in making the agent execute malicious commands, the sandbox limits the blast radius.
key_strategies.implementation: Docker sandbox: --network=none, --read-only, --tmpfs /tmp:size=100m, --memory=512m, --cpus=1, --security-opt=no-new-privileges, --cap-drop=ALL. For stronger isolation: gVisor or Firecracker microVMs. Read-only workspace mount: -v /workspace:/workspace:ro.

key_strategies.name: Instruction Hierarchy with Content Boundary Markers
key_strategies.description: Establish a clear precedence order: system prompt > application logic > user input > external data. Use explicit delimiters to separate trusted instructions from untrusted data. The model should never override system-level constraints based on content from lower-priority sources.
key_strategies.implementation: Wrap all external content in UNTRUSTED DATA markers. Modern models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 support explicit instruction hierarchy through API parameters. Example: `---BEGIN UNTRUSTED DATA--- ${userCode} ---END UNTRUSTED DATA---`

key_strategies.name: Least-Privilege Agent Configuration
key_strategies.description: Agents should not inherit full developer credentials. Run under constrained service accounts with scoped permissions. Define allowlists for permitted tools, file paths, and API endpoints.
key_strategies.implementation: Service account with read-only access to specific repos, no write access to production, no access to credential stores. Tool allowlist: only permit known-safe tools. File path allowlist: restrict write access to specific directories. Shell command allowlist: block dangerous operations (curl to external hosts, eval, exec).

key_strategies.name: Approval Gates for High-Risk Actions
key_strategies.description: Require explicit human approval before file writes, shell commands, network requests to external services, and credential access. This is the ultimate backstop: even if all automated defenses fail, a human reviewer can catch malicious actions before they execute.
key_strategies.implementation: Calibrate which actions require approval. File writes to new locations, shell commands with network destinations, package installs from untrusted sources, and credential access should always require human-in-the-loop approval. Use rate limiting to prevent approval fatigue.

key_strategies.name: Canary Tokens and Honeytokens in Repositories
key_strategies.description: Embed fake credentials and API keys in repositories as canary tokens. If an agent accesses or exfiltrates these tokens, the security team is immediately alerted. This provides early warning of successful prompt injection.
key_strategies.implementation: Deploy canary tokens (e.g., Thinkst Canarytokens) in README files, configuration files, and environment variable templates. Monitor for access. On alert: investigate agent activity, review execution logs, rotate real credentials.

key_strategies.name: Runtime Defense: StruQ and SecAlign
key_strategies.description: Academic research shows StruQ (separating prompts and data channels) achieves <2% attack success, and SecAlign (preference optimization) reduces attack success from 96% to 2%. These are emerging runtime defenses that should be evaluated for production deployment.
key_strategies.implementation: StruQ: architecturally separate instruction channels from data channels so injected content cannot override system instructions. SecAlign: fine-tune models with preference optimization to reject injection attempts. ETDI: implement cryptographic identity for tools with immutable versioning and OAuth 2.0 scopes.

key_strategies.name: Audit Logging and Anomaly Detection
key_strategies.description: Log all agent-executed actions: file reads/writes, shell commands, network requests, API calls. Use ML-based anomaly detection to identify behavioral deviations from baseline patterns. Injection attacks often produce anomalous patterns of activity.
key_strategies.implementation: Log every tool call with timestamp, tool name, arguments, and result. Establish baseline per-agent behavior (normal tool call frequency, typical file access patterns). Flag deviations: sudden spike in tool calls, access to unusual files, network requests to unknown destinations.

defense_layers_summary.layer_1: Input Validation — Sanitize all external content before agent processes it
defense_layers_summary.layer_2: Output Filtering — Validate agent outputs before execution against allowlist
defense_layers_summary.layer_3: Privilege Separation — Least-privilege service accounts, scoped permissions
defense_layers_summary.layer_4: Sandboxing — Docker/gVisor/Firecracker with network isolation, read-only FS
defense_layers_summary.layer_5: Content Boundary Markers — Delimiters between trusted instructions and untrusted data
defense_layers_summary.layer_6: Instruction Hierarchy — System > app logic > user > external data precedence
defense_layers_summary.layer_7: Canary Tokens — Honeytokens that trigger alerts on access
defense_layers_summary.layer_8: Rate Limiting — Per-session and per-minute tool call caps
defense_layers_summary.layer_9: Anomaly Detection — ML-based behavioral monitoring against baseline
defense_layers_summary.layer_10: Human-in-the-Loop — Approval gates for high-risk actions

key_takeaways: The 'Clean Repo' attack is not vendor-specific — it exploits a fundamental architectural trust gap in all AI coding agents
Filtering and warning banners are insufficient as standalone controls against adaptive prompt injection
Defense must be defense-in-depth: no single layer is sufficient, but 10 layers together provide meaningful protection
Pre-scan repositories before agent execution is the most critical pre-setup defense
Sandboxed execution with network isolation limits blast radius even when injection succeeds
Instruction hierarchy and content boundary markers are the most effective model-level defenses
Human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk actions is the ultimate backstop
Treat every unfamiliar repository, setup script, package file, and README as untrusted input
Shadow AI (unsanctioned agent tooling) dramatically increases risk because it bypasses governance controls
